knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)

Every error and warning `sigdots()` can give, what it means, and what to do; followed by the
questions users ask most. Messages are quoted as the package prints them.

## Errors before anything is computed

SigDoTS checks all inputs first, so these errors appear within a second.

**"`x` has 2000 rows but `coords` has 3639. `x` has 3639 columns, so it is probably one row per gene; use t(x) to give one row per spot."**
Expression matrices from most tools have genes in rows. SigDoTS wants spots in rows:

```r
fit <- sigdots(t(x), coords, K0 = 10)
```

**"`x` has 3500 rows (spots) but `coords` has 3639."**
The two matrices describe different sets of spots. Usually some spots were filtered from
one and not the other; subset both to the same spots, in the same order:

```r
common <- intersect(rownames(x), rownames(coords))
fit <- sigdots(x[common, ], coords[common, ], K0 = 10)
```

**"`coords` must have exactly two columns (it has 3)."**
Keep the two columns that hold the positions, for example `coords[, c("x", "y")]` or
`coords[, c("pxl_col_in_fullres", "pxl_row_in_fullres")]`.

**"At least half of the spots share their coordinates with another spot ..."**
The coordinates are not the spots' positions (for example all zeros, or a column of
indices). Check which columns you passed.

**"Give K0, the number of candidate domains (or `candidate_labels`)."**
`K0` has no default, because it depends on your tissue. Choose more candidate domains than
domains you expect; see "How do I choose K0?" below.

**"K0 = 5, but `candidate_labels` has 8 distinct labels."**
When you give labels, `K0` is their number of distinct values; leave `K0` out.

**"cluster_method = "banksy" needs the Bioconductor package(s) Banksy, SingleCellExperiment, SummarizedExperiment. Install with: ..."**
BANKSY and BayesSpace are not installed with SigDoTS. Run the printed `BiocManager::install()`
command once, then rerun.

**"spatial_method = "exact" would need about 42.9 GiB of memory at a test on 32,000 spots, more than max_exact_memory_gib = 16. Use spatial_method = "vecchia", or ... raise it ..."**
The exact spatial computation stores an n x n matrix for a part of the tree with n spots.
Use the default `spatial_method = "vecchia"`, or, on a machine with enough memory,
`control = sigdots_control(max_exact_memory_gib = 64)`.

## Warnings at the end of a run

The run completed; the warning tells you about parts of the result that need attention.
`summary(fit)` shows the parts concerned with their node numbers.

**"The spatial parameters could not be estimated at 2 part(s) of the tree (too few spots), so these parts were not tested and their spots have no domain: node 7 (48 spots, candidate domains 3,4); node 8 (48 spots, candidate domains 1,2). A smaller K0 makes the parts larger; see summary() and vignette("faq")."**
To estimate the spatial correlation at a part of the tree, SigDoTS uses pairs of spots that
belong to the same candidate domain, sorted by distance. A part with few spots does not have
enough such pairs (on a regular grid, about 80 spots are needed). SigDoTS leaves that part
untested, still tests the rest of the tree, marks the part `[!] NOT TESTED` in the printed
tree and grey in `plot(fit)`, and gives its spots `NA` in `domains(fit)`.

What to do: use fewer candidate domains (a smaller `K0`), so that each part of the tree is
larger; or, if the untested part is small and you accept it as it is, treat its spots as one
domain yourself. Do not interpret an untested part as "not significant": it was not tested.

**"At 1 part(s) of the tree, the simulated datasets whose top split left fewer than min_child_size = 8 spots on a side outnumbered the valid ones, so these parts were not tested and their spots have no domain: node 9 (120 spots, candidate domains 2,5; 31 simulated datasets replaced). See summary() and vignette("faq")."**
A split of the data is tested only when both of its sides have at least `min_child_size`
spots, so SigDoTS asks the same of every simulated dataset. One whose top split leaves fewer
spots on a side is replaced by a new one and is not counted; `summary(fit)` lists the tests
where this happened, with the number replaced. It has been seen where the spots of a part
lie in many small separate pieces and the simulated datasets are grouped with a method that
uses each spot's neighbourhood (BANKSY): the spots of a small isolated piece share most of
their neighbours and tend to be grouped together even in simulated data without any domain,
so the top split cuts off that piece. When the replaced simulated datasets outnumber the
valid ones, SigDoTS does not decide the test from the ones that remain: it leaves the part
untested, still tests the rest of the tree, marks the part `[!] NOT TESTED`, and gives its
spots `NA` in `domains(fit)`.

What to do: look at where the spots of that part lie (`plot(fit, type = "candidates")`).
Fewer candidate domains (a smaller `K0`) usually give parts whose spots lie together. Do not
interpret an untested part as "not significant": it was not tested.

**"At 1 test(s) the estimated spatial range ell is at the upper end of its allowed range (40): node(s) 8. Rerun with a wider range, for example control = sigdots_control(ell_range = c(0.3, 80)); see vignette("faq")."**
`ell` says how far the spatial correlation of the noise reaches, in units of the distance
between neighbouring spots. SigDoTS searches it between 0.3 and 40 by default. When the
estimate sits at 40, the true value may be larger, and a single-domain model with too short
a range makes splits look clearer than they are. Rerun with a wider range:

```r
fit <- sigdots(x, coords, K0 = 10, control = sigdots_control(ell_range = c(0.3, 80)))
```

If the estimate moves to the new upper end again, the tissue has correlation over very long
distances relative to the spot spacing; look at `plot(fit, type = "correlogram", test = 8)`.

**summary() says "Spots in separate pieces on the 6-nearest-neighbour graph (joined by their closest spots for the tree)", for example "[11] 308 spots: pieces of 242, 49, 14 and 3 single spots"**
This no longer stops a run. When the spots of a part of the tree fall into separate pieces on
the 6-nearest-neighbour graph (a layer cut by a fold; a few spots whose neighbours all belong
to other candidate domains), the pieces are joined by their closest spots before the tree is built, so
that every grouping of a simulated dataset has a connected tree. `summary()` lists the parts
where this happened, with the piece sizes. If a detached piece is a different piece of tissue
rather than a fragment of the same layer, analyse it separately (subset its spots).

**"At 1 part(s) of the tree the test would need more than B_cap = 5000 simulated datasets: node(s) 23. These parts were not tested and are reported as domains. To test them, raise B_cap in sigdots_control()."**
A test on m of the n spots uses the level `alpha * (m - 1) / (n - 1)`; for a small part of a
very large sample this is tiny, and reaching it needs more than `B_cap` simulated datasets.
Raise `B_cap` (`sigdots_control(B_cap = 20000)`), at the cost of time, or accept that part as
a domain.

## Questions

### How do I choose K0?

`K0` is the number of candidate domains. SigDoTS merges candidate domains into domains; it never
splits an candidate domain. So each candidate domain must lie inside one true domain, and `K0`
must be larger than the number of domains you expect. Twice the expected number is a
reasonable start. If `K0` is much too large, the lower parts of the tree become too small to
test (see the first warning above); if it is too small, two true domains may share an
candidate domain and can never be separated. Running SigDoTS with two or three values of `K0`
and comparing `plot(fit)` is a good check: domains that are real appear for every `K0`.

### I have a Seurat object / a SpatialExperiment / a Scanpy file. What do I pass?

Pass the object itself: `sigdots(obj, K0 = 10)` for a Seurat object (normalised with
`NormalizeData()`, variable genes set with `FindVariableFeatures()`), `sigdots(spe, K0 = 10,
genes = hvg)` for a SpatialExperiment with a `logcounts` assay. A Scanpy `.h5ad` file can be
read into a SingleCellExperiment with `zellkonverter::readH5AD()`; then give the positions:
`sigdots(sce, coords = reducedDim(sce, "spatial"), K0 = 10)`. `add_domains(obj, fit)` writes
the domains back into the object. Details and runnable examples: `vignette("own-data")`.

### Can I use labels from Seurat, BANKSY or another tool?

Yes: `sigdots(x, coords, candidate_labels = labels)`, or, for an object, the name of the metadata
column, `sigdots(obj, candidate_labels = "seurat_clusters")`. The tree is built from your labels.
The simulated datasets, however, are grouped with `cluster_method` (k-means by default),
because SigDoTS must cluster each simulated dataset the same way every time. The test is
therefore calibrated for labels made the way `cluster_method` makes them; when your labels
come from a very different method, read the p-values with this in mind. If your tool is
BANKSY or BayesSpace, prefer `cluster_method = "banksy"` or `"bayesspace"`, which applies the
same method to the data and to the simulated datasets.

### Why are the p-values so coarse (0.05, 0.033, 0.0909, 1)?

Each test uses only as many simulated datasets as needed to decide: 10 by default, raised
to `ceiling(1 / level) - 1` (19 at the first test with `alpha = 0.05`) and stopped as soon
as the decision cannot change. With B datasets the p-value is a multiple of 1/(B + 1). The
decision (split or not) is what the test establishes; the p-value is reported for
completeness. If you want finer p-values, raise `B_min` and `B_max`, for example
`B_min = 100, B_max = 100`, which costs about ten times the run time at every test. More
simulated datasets also give a true split that is only moderately clear a better chance of
being kept; the error guarantee holds either way.

### Can the tests of a large tree run faster?

The lower tests of a large tree have small levels, and a Monte Carlo test needs about
1 / level simulated datasets to keep a split (about 200 for a part with a tenth of the
spots). `pvalue_method = "normal_adaptive"` computes the p-value from a normal distribution
fitted to the simulated statistics instead, with 10 simulated datasets per test, or 50 when
the result is near the level (`normal_n_initial`, `normal_n_refine`). It relies on the
simulated statistics being roughly normal; the Monte Carlo p-value, the default, makes no such
assumption.

### How many genes should I give, and how should they be normalised?

Use normalised, log-transformed expression (for example log(1 + counts per 10,000)) and the
most variable genes, typically 1,000 to 3,000. All genes you give enter the split statistic
with equal weight per unit of variance; genes with larger variance count more. If you want
every gene to count equally, scale the columns of `x` to unit variance first. Do not give
raw counts.

### My tissue may be one domain. What does SigDoTS report then?

The first test, on all spots, is not significant; SigDoTS reports one domain, and the tree
shows `no split` at the top with your `K0` candidate domains under it.

### Will I get the same result again?

Yes, with the same data, arguments and `seed` (default 1), on any number of cores. SigDoTS
also puts the random-number state of your session back when it returns. Changing `K0`,
the normalisation or the gene set changes the candidate domains and therefore the tree.

### How many cores should I use?

`n_cores` runs the simulated datasets of one test in parallel; the gain is largest at the
first test, which uses 19 datasets at `alpha = 0.05`. On Linux and macOS use as many cores
as you have, up to about 20. On Windows SigDoTS runs on one core and says so.

### How long will it take, and how much memory?

See the table in the README (or `vignette("own-data")`). For orientation: 900 spots take
about 20 seconds on one core; 2,500 spots about 4 minutes on 10 cores; 10,000 spots about
20 minutes on 10 cores with the exact computation. Memory grows with the square of the
number of spots in the largest tested part; for samples above about 20,000 spots use the
default Vecchia approximation and a computer with enough memory (the spatial-parameter
estimation alone used 7 GiB at 20,000 spots and 29 GiB at 40,000).

### What does `=> DOMAIN 2` mean in the printed tree?

That part of the tree was not split further and is the second final domain. Domains are
numbered from left to right in the tree; `domains(fit)` gives the number of each spot.

### What do `eta` and `ell` mean?

They describe the spatial correlation of the noise that the single-domain model assumes,
estimated anew at every test from pairs of spots in the same candidate domain: `eta` is the
share of the noise variance that is correlated between spots (0 = none, 1 = all), `ell` is
how far that correlation reaches, in spot spacings (Matérn 3/2 correlation). They are
nuisance parameters: SigDoTS estimates them so that the simulated data are as spatially
smooth as the real data, which is what makes the test fair; they are not findings about the
tissue.

### On Linux, `library(SigDoTS)` fails with "libglpk.so.40: cannot open shared object file"

The igraph package, which SigDoTS uses to build the tree, needs the GLPK library of the operating
system, and minimal Linux installations (for example small Docker images) do not have it. Install
the system libraries igraph uses, then reinstall igraph:

```bash
sudo apt-get install libglpk-dev libgmp-dev libxml2-dev     # Ubuntu, Debian
sudo dnf install glpk-devel gmp-devel libxml2-devel          # Fedora
```

```r
install.packages("igraph")
```

On Windows and macOS the igraph binaries from CRAN contain the library and nothing extra is
needed.

### Where do I report a problem?

Once the repository is public, open an issue on GitHub with the output of
`sessionInfo()`, the exact call, and the full message. Until then, write to the maintainer.
